===== FILE 19930__1.pdf =====
September 2, 2025 
 
Submitted electronically via regulations.gov 
 
 
Steven L. Lieberman, MD, MBA, FACHE, FACP  
Acting Under Secretary for Health 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
Re: Reproductive Health Services, 38 CFR Part 17 (RIN 2900-AR57) 
 
Dear Dr. Lieberman: 
 
On behalf of the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine (SMFM) and our members, we write in strong 
opposition to the US Department of Veterans Affairs’ (VA) Reproductive Health Services Proposed Rule 
(the “Proposed Rule”). The Proposed Rule would eliminate counseling for abortion care and effectively 
ban abortion care for veterans and their family members, including those with high-risk pregnancies. We 
urge you to rescind the Proposed Rule and ensure veterans have access to the care they need.  
 
Founded in 1977, SMFM is the medical professional society for maternal-fetal medicine subspecialists, 
who are obstetricians with additional training in high-risk pregnancies. SMFM represents more than 
6,500 members who care for high-risk pregnant people and provides education, promotes research, and 
engages in advocacy to advance optimal and equitable perinatal outcomes for all people who desire and 
experience pregnancy.  
 
As physicians who provide care to individuals experiencing high-risk pregnancies, the Society is 
particularly concerned with access to the full spectrum of reproductive health services, including 
abortion care. Individuals with high-risk pregnancies are more likely to experience medical complications 
– for themselves, their fetus(es), or both – that can lead to increased maternal and perinatal morbidity 
and mortality. In some instances, abortion care may be required to protect the life or health of an 
individual with a complicated pregnancy. It is essential that all medically appropriate options are 
available to patients and clinicians to guarantee positive health outcomes throughout pregnancy.1 
 
I. 
Abortion care is safe, common, and an essential component of healthcare 
 
SMFM stands with the medical community and recognizes that abortion care is safe, common, and an 
essential component of healthcare.2  In 2024, there were more than 1,038,000 clinician-provided

2 Forbes, L. et al. Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine Position Statement: Access to abortion care, Obstetrics & 
Gynecology, 231(1), July 2024, doi: 10.1016/j.ajog.2024.04.006. 

abortions in the US states without total bans on abortion care.3 Approximately one in four women will 
have an abortion by the age of 45, and approximately 55% of people who have received abortion care 
have previously given birth.4 
 
Available medical evidence clearly demonstrates that abortion care is safe.5 Complications are 
exceedingly rare, occurring in around 2% of cases, and most complications are minor and easily 
treatable. 6 Major complications are even more rare, occurring in no more than 0.5% of instances. 7 By 
contrast, childbirth is considerably more dangerous – the risk of death associated with childbirth is 
approximately 14 times higher than the risk of death associated with abortion care. 8  
 
II. The Proposed Rule would harm veterans and their loved ones 
 
The VA has a responsibility to support our country’s veterans – in fact, they have clear directives from 
Congress to “promote, preserve, or restore the health” of veterans. 9 This inherently includes those who 
may need access to abortion care.  
 
There are more than 2 million women veterans in the US,10 and based on the American Census Survey 
2023 1-Year Estimates, approximately 20% of those women veterans live in the 12 states with total 
abortion bans.11 These numbers will only increase in the coming years, as women are the fastest 
growing cohort within the veteran community.12 Under the Proposed Rule, veterans in these states – as 
well as the hundreds of thousands of others living in other states with restrictive abortion policies – will 
be forced to either remain pregnant or join the tens of thousands of civilians who must travel out of

state to access needed care.13 However, the harm caused by Proposed Rule will not be limited to 
veterans in states with abortion bans and restrictions – the Proposed Rule will impact all veterans who 
utilize care provided through the VA or covered by the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the 
Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA). 
 
Veterans who are able to access care outside the VA system will undoubtedly face steep costs. For 
veterans who must find care out of state, not only will they have to pay for travel and overnight stays, 
but they may also need to account for childcare and unpaid time off. Additionally, abortion care 
becomes more expensive the later it is performed.14 This is especially true for those with high-risk 
pregnancies, as any pregnancy-related care becomes more complicated and thus expensive in high-risk 
cases. These costs will impact not only those veterans who must travel, but also those who can access 
in-state care but rely on the CHAMPVA for health insurance. Female veterans are already more likely to 
live in poverty than their male counterparts – these costs will only exacerbate this reality.15 
 
Additionally, the Proposed Rule will either lead to delays in care or force veterans to remain pregnant, 
both of which pose significant health risks. Pregnancy is not a benign condition – even uncomplicated 
pregnancies cause extensive stress on the body and can exacerbate underlying conditions or lead to new 
health issues. For example, conditions like Alport Syndrome, lupus, and pulmonary hypertension can all 
be made worse by pregnancy. Additionally, labor and delivery pose risks to pregnant patients – veterans 
included – such as hemorrhage, placenta accreta spectrum (when the placenta cannot detach during 
childbirth), and emergency hysterectomy.16  
 
By delaying care or forcing veterans to remain pregnant, the Proposed Rule will inevitably lead to long-
term health consequences and even death. In the US, two mothers die due to pregnancy-related causes 
each day.17 Furthermore, maternal morbidity rates continue to rise. Life threatening and near miss 
severe maternal morbidity is estimated to occur in approximately 50,000 to 60,000 deliveries per year 
and has a profound effect on patients and families.18 It is thus imperative that veterans readily have 
access to abortion care to protect their health and their lives.

III. The Proposed Rule interferes with the patient-clinician relationship and is at odds with 
clinicians’ ethical obligations 
 
Policies that regulate medical care should be based on scientific evidence, best practices, and preserve 
the patient-clinician relationship. This relationship is established on trust and the ability to counsel 
honestly and confidentially about what is in a patient’s best medical interest based on the best available 
medical science and the patient’s lived experience.19 
 
Preventing clinicians from providing comprehensive counseling and medically indicated care inherently 
compromises clinician judgement and is antithetical to medical ethics. As specialists in high-risk 
pregnancies, our members counsel patients through a series of decisions that require careful 
consideration, helping them weigh life-threatening risks and uncertainties to identify the outcome that 
is best for them, their pregnancy, and their family. Sometimes abortion care is what they choose. 
Healthcare professionals have a duty to make sure every patient gets the information and care they 
need. The Proposed Rule would prohibit our members from fulfilling this duty. 
 
Abortion care is healthcare, and all individuals – including veterans and their family members – must be 
able to access the full spectrum of perinatal and reproductive health services. It is critical to safeguard 
and lift restrictions that limit access to abortion care, especially with ongoing legislative and legal attacks 
on abortion rights across the country. SMFM is committed to protecting access to abortion care and 
ensuring that individuals receive high-quality and equitable perinatal and reproductive healthcare. We 
thus urge you to rescind the Proposed Rule. 
 
Please do not hesitate to contact Samantha Berg, SMFM’s Advocacy Manager, at sberg@smfm.org 
should you have questions. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
 
 
Sindhu K. Srinivas, MD, MSCE 
 
 
 
Christina J. Wurster, MBA, CAE
